_readme: How a scanned sheet is read. Edit THIS file to change the OCR engine or tune it.
Precedence (lowest -> highest): code defaults < this file < environment variables < database settings table.
After editing, either restart the app, or run:  python cli.py sync-model-config
That command pushes these values into the database settings table so they win over stale DB rows.
engine: 'auto' | 'paddle' | 'tesseract'
auto     = a PDF's own text layer first, then PaddleOCR, then Tesseract
paddle   = force PaddleOCR (falls back to Tesseract on hard failure)
tesseract= classic local OCR only, never calls PaddleOCR
Every engine here runs on this machine. A quality record is never sent to a
hosted service to be read, which is the point: a plant that will not let its
inspection sheets leave the building can still have them read.
PaddleOCR is the accurate one and the only engine that keeps the document's
structure - tables stay tables, so a filled format still looks like the format.
It is an optional dependency:  pip install -r requirements-ocr.txt
Models download on first use (about 200 MB) and are cached in ~/.paddleocr.
table_recognition: recover each table from where the recognised words sit
on the page. The text detector already reports every line's box, so this
costs nothing and is enough for a ruled form like an inspection sheet.
table_model: use PaddleOCR's own table pipeline instead, which detects
cells with two RT-DETR models. More accurate on a wildly irregular table.
On a CPU it took over ten minutes for a single page - switch it on only
with a GPU (use_gpu) and a reason.
models: 'mobile' or 'server'. The server pair is more accurate on a
difficult scan and about ten times slower on a CPU - 225 seconds for one
inspection sheet here, against seconds for mobile. Use server with a GPU.
